hooks.text: Astronomers built a massive deep-space telescope pointed straight down through Earth.
One of the world's most powerful telescopes points straight into the ground.
A cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice is looking straight through our planet.

title: The Deep-Space Telescope Pointed Into Earth
description: Beneath the South Pole, the IceCube observatory turns a cubic kilometer of ice into a telescope that looks straight down through our planet.

beats.text: Astronomers built a massive deep-space telescope pointed straight down through Earth.

queries: IceCube Neutrino Observatory building South Pole
Amundsen Scott South Pole Station IceCube exterior

beats.text: Beneath the South Pole, researchers turned a cubic kilometer of ice into the IceCube observatory.
beats.visual: diagram of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory cubic kilometer detector array, 2010

beats.text: Hot-water drills melted holes 2,500 meters deep, freezing 5,000 optical sensors into the ice.
beats.visual: photograph of an IceCube Digital Optical Module sensor before deployment, 2005

beats.text: Completed in 2010, the array captures neutrinos traveling in straight lines across the cosmos.
beats.visual: hot water drilling tower deployed on the polar plateau, 2010
queries: IceCube hot water drill South Pole
Enhanced Hot Water Drill IceCube Antarctica

beats.text: Atmospheric cosmic rays swamp neutrino signals by roughly one million to one.
beats.visual: computer simulation of atmospheric cosmic-ray particle showers entering polar ice, 2011
queries: IceCube cosmic ray particle event display

beats.text: To block that noise, IceCube uses the solid Earth as a physical shield.
beats.visual: diagram showing neutrinos passing through the Earth to the South Pole detector, 2013

beats.text: The detector tracks upward-traveling particles from neutrinos that passed entirely through Earth.
beats.visual: visualization of an upward-moving neutrino event lighting up IceCube optical sensors, 2017

beats.text: In September 2017, it pinpointed a neutrino from a blazar 3.7 billion light-years away.
beats.visual: artist concept of relativistic jet erupting from blazar TXS 0506+056, 2018

beats.text: To look into deep space, scientists had to aim straight through our planet.
beats.visual: aerial photograph of the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station landscape, 2018
